record.paper_title: Reusing Space: Techniques and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can techniques based on reusing space be turned into evidence against natural cryptographic objects or primitives?

evidence.quote: Problem 33. Show evidence against objects in cryptography based on techniques in reusing space.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In computational complexity, recent advances on space-bounded computation have produced "space-reuse" techniques (such as catalytic computation and Williams-type simulations showing TIME[t] ⊆ SPACE[√(t log t)]) which yield surprisingly efficient algorithms that reuse memory while preserving the contents of auxiliary tapes. A cryptographic primitive (for example, a one-way function, pseudorandom generator, pseudorandom function, collision-resistant hash function, or public-key encryption scheme) is said to be "broken" by an algorithm A if A computes the corresponding inverse/distinguishing/collision task with non-negligible advantage in resources substantially smaller than those guaranteed by the security assumption.

Problem: Exhibit a natural cryptographic primitive P (e.g., a candidate one-way function, pseudorandom generator, or hash function from the standard cryptographic literature) together with an algorithm A obtained via space-reuse techniques (catalytic computation, simulation of time by small space, or related reusable-workspace methods) such that A provides nontrivial evidence against the conjectured security of P — for instance, by giving a space-efficient attack that contradicts the standard hardness assumption, or by showing that the existence of P would imply the failure of a known space-reuse simulation. Equivalently: turn space-reuse techniques into concrete evidence (e.g., an attack, a non-black-box reduction, or a barrier) against the security of natural cryptographic objects.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem asks for the use of space-reuse techniques (catalytic computation, Williams-style time-space simulations) to provide evidence against cryptographic primitives. No published work appears to have accomplished this; it is posed as an open direction in recent surveys on reusing space, and we found no sources claiming a resolution.

status_evidence.snippet: Survey on space-reuse techniques (catalytic computation, time-space simulations) and a list of open problems including connections to cryptography.
status_evidence.claim: The question of turning space-reuse techniques into evidence against cryptographic objects is listed as an open problem in this survey.
